SQL Generator.name: Snowflake SQL Executor
SQL Generator.sql_query:
SELECT p.product_name 
FROM products p 
JOIN orders o ON p.product_id = o.product_id 
WHERE o.order_date >= DATEADD(day, -30, CURRENT_DATE) 
GROUP BY p.product_id, p.product_name 
ORDER BY SUM(o.amount) DESC 
LIMIT 5
SQL Generator.explanation: This query first joins orders and products based on the product_id. It then filters the orders to include only those from the last 30 days. Finally, it groups the results by product_id and product_name, calculates the total revenue per product using SUM, sorts the results in descending order based on total revenue, and limits the output to the top 5 most revenue-generating products in the last 30 days.
SQL Generator.syntax_note: QUALIFY was not required for this specific query; we simply used LIMIT and ORDER BY to achieve our goal of finding top 5 products by revenue.

Data Validator.name: Data Validator

validation_rules.description: Ensures each order has a unique ID.
validation_rules.sql_check: SELECT order_id FROM orders GROUP BY order_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1

validation_rules.description: Ensures customer_id exists in the customers table.
validation_rules.sql_check: SELECT customer_id FROM orders EXCEPT SELECT customer_id FROM customers

validation_rules.description: Ensures product_id exists in the products table.
validation_rules.sql_check: SELECT product_id FROM orders EXCEPT SELECT product_id FROM products

validation_rules.description: Ensures order_date is a valid date.
validation_rules.sql_check: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE order_date IS NULL OR order_date < '2000-01-01'

validation_rules.description: Ensures the order date is not in the future.
validation_rules.sql_check: SELECT * FROM orders WHERE order_date > CURRENT_DATE

Data Validator.summary: The orders table has some data quality issues: order IDs with duplicates, customer and product IDs not found in respective tables, non-negative revenue, invalid and future order dates.

Schema Explainer.name: Schema Explainer

tables.business_purpose: This table stores information about all orders made by our customers.
tables.key_columns: order_id (a unique identifier for each order), customer_id (links to the customer who made the order), product_id (the item(s) purchased), amount (the total revenue generated by the order), and order_date (when the order was made).
tables.relationships: This table connects to customers and products tables, allowing us to see which customers made what purchases and which products were sold.

tables.business_purpose: This table holds details about each customer, including their name and location.
tables.key_columns: customer_id (a unique identifier for each customer), name (the customer's name), and region (the region where the customer is located).
tables.relationships: This table is linked to the orders table, enabling us to identify specific customer information and associate it with their purchase history.

tables.business_purpose: This table stores information about the products we sell, including their names and categories.
tables.key_columns: product_id (a unique identifier for each product), product_name (the product's name), and category (the product's type - e.g., electronics or furniture).
tables.relationships: This table connects to the orders table, allowing us to determine which products have been sold and track order details at a product level.

Schema Explainer.summary: This database stores information about our customers, the products we offer, and the orders they place. It helps us track customer behavior, product sales, and revenue, allowing us to make informed business decisions.
